Hashabiah
hash-a-bī'ä
n. (a chief of the Levites in the return under Ezra, entrusted with the holy vessels; a name borne also by rulers, officers and singers of the tribe of Levi)
From Hebrew Chashabyah, the LORD hath considered or whom the LORD regardeth, from chashab, to think, reckon, esteem, with Yah. The same verb is the one Genesis uses when the LORD counted Abraham's faith to him for righteousness.

Biblical Definition

Hashabiah is one of the working names of the tribe of Levi, and the men who bore it turn up wherever something had to be carried, governed or sung. In Ezra's caravan he is one of the Merarite chiefs recruited at the river Ahava: “And Hashabiah, and with him Jeshaiah of the sons of Merari, his brethren and their sons, twenty” (Ezr 8:19), and then one of the twelve to whom the treasure was committed for a journey of four months without an escort: “Then I separated twelve of the chief of the priests, Sherebiah, Hashabiah, and ten of their brethren with them” (Ezr 8:24). In Nehemiah he is a civil ruler taking his turn on the wall: “Next unto him repaired Hashabiah, the ruler of the half part of Keilah, in his part” (Neh 3:17). He is among the chief of the Levites appointed “to praise and to give thanks, according to the commandment of David the man of God, ward over against ward” (Neh 12:24). An earlier Hashabiah of the Hebronites commanded seventeen hundred officers west of Jordan “in all the business of the LORD, and in the service of the king” (1Ch 26:30) — a phrase which is itself a small doctrine of vocation, the sacred and the civil work of one man named in one breath.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Hashabiah; in sacred history it is the name of several Levites, one of whom carried the treasure up from Babylon with Ezra.

HASHABIAH, n. Whom the LORD regardeth; a proper name borne by several Levites.

One of the chief men of the sons of Merari who went up with Ezra from Babylon.

He was among the twelve to whom the silver and the gold and the vessels were committed.

In Nehemiah he is the ruler of the half part of Keilah, and repaired his portion of the wall.

A Hashabiah of the Hebronites was over the officers of Israel westward of Jordan.

Key Scripture

Ezr 8:19 — "And Hashabiah, and with him Jeshaiah of the sons of Merari, his brethren and their sons, twenty;"

Ezr 8:24 — "Then I separated twelve of the chief of the priests, Sherebiah, Hashabiah, and ten of their brethren with them,"

Neh 3:17 — "After him repaired the Levites, Rehum the son of Bani. Next unto him repaired Hashabiah, the ruler of the half part of Keilah, in his part."

1Ch 26:30 — "And of the Hebronites, Hashabiah and his brethren, men of valour, a thousand and seven hundred, were officers among them of Israel on this side Jordan westward in all the business of the LORD, and in the service of the king."

Modern Corruption

There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is that the business of the LORD and the service of the king are two lawful callings that God has given to the same men, and that the church impoverishes itself by grading one above the other.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Hashabiah is a Levite of the lists and nobody has contested him. What the Chronicler's phrase sets against a persistent churchly instinct is the flat pairing of “the business of the LORD” with “the service of the king” as the joint description of one man's office. The same Levites who sang the psalms judged causes, kept treasuries, commanded officers and rebuilt a wall. Nehemiah's roll of the builders is a roll of goldsmiths, apothecaries, merchants, rulers of districts and priests, each repairing over against his own house.

The principle to recover is the doctrine of vocation as the Reformers recovered it. The medieval church divided life into the religious and the secular and reserved holiness for the cloister; Luther and Calvin answered that the milkmaid and the magistrate serve God in their callings as truly as the preacher in his. Paul states it as a rule for everyone: “whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God” (1Co 10:31), and “whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men” (Col 3:23). Hashabiah carried silver four months across a dangerous road because it was the business of the LORD, and he counted the mile-markers as carefully as he sang the psalm.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Chashabyah (H2811), the LORD hath regarded; chashab (H2803), to think, reckon, impute; Yah (H3050), the LORD; mela'kah (H4399), business, work; Merari (H4847), Merari.

expand to see more

Hebrew Chashabyah (H2811) — Hashabiah; whom the LORD regardeth.

Hebrew chashab (H2803) — to reckon, impute; the verb of Genesis 15:6.

Hebrew Yah (H3050) — the LORD; the divine element of the name.

Hebrew mela'kah (H4399) — business, work; ‘the business of the LORD’.

Hebrew Merari (H4847) — Merari; the Levitical house he belonged to.

Usage

"“Hashabiah, and with him Jeshaiah of the sons of Merari” — ministers found for a journey."

"“The ruler of the half part of Keilah, in his part” — a magistrate with a trowel."

"“In all the business of the LORD, and in the service of the king” — two callings, one man."
